## A Implementation and Training Details

Architecture. Each candidate enters the head as one vector of the head's hidden width, formed by summing four terms. The first is the target's input embedding of the candidate token, held frozen and projected down. The second is the drafter's hidden state at that slot, projected down and shared by the slot's K candidates. The third is a two-layer network over five scalars describing the drafter's confidence in the candidate, all read from its distribution at that slot: the log-probability and the probability under the full vocabulary, the log-probability gap to the slot's most likely token, the rank normalized to [0,1], and an indicator for being the slot's top choice. The fourth is a pair of learned tables, one indexed by slot and one by rank. The target state that every candidate is later fused with is formed separately: the target's hidden states that produced the last verified token, collapsed across five captured layers, normalized, and projected to the same width.

The head itself is a two-layer bidirectional Transformer over the $( B-1 ) \times K$ candidate lattice, attending over all of it at once, with hidden width 1024, eight attention heads, and a feed-forward width of 2048, using RMSNorm and SiLU activations. Beyond the slot table, position enters through two attention biases learned per head and added to the attention logits, one indexed by the signed slot distance between a pair and one marking pairs of candidates that occupy the same slot. Only after the Transformer is each candidate combined with that target state, by concatenating the candidate state, the target state, and their elementwise product, and projecting the result back down to the head's width through a single linear layer followed by a SiLU. This is the one concatenation in the head, everything else being a sum. Two linear heads then emit the out and in vectors of Section 3.2, each of dimension $d_{e}$ and normalized to unit norm, and a third emits the anchor's single out vector. Objective. The DFlash cross-entropy of Eq. (5) is applied at every slot, whereas the LiLiCorr terms are evaluated only on the oracle prefix, the maximal run of leading slots in which the groundtruth token is present in the candidate pool. Slots beyond the first coverage miss contribute to none of the three terms.

Serving. We fuse top-$K$ candidate extraction and vocabulary-wide logit normalization into a single kernel, compile the matching and selection step, and use wide CUDA graphs that fold candidate pooling and reranking into a single replay. The same level of optimization is applied to Domino's correction loop. Table 3 gives the resulting per-block cost of each head and is the source of the figures quoted in Section 4.1.

Isolating the head. Table 3 is obtained by subtraction. Every benchmark run under greedy decoding reports throughput and acceptance length, and their ratio is the wall-clock time of one verification block. The DFlash control is the same system with no reranking at all, and its block takes 8.87 ms on Qwen3-8B and 5.88 ms on Qwen3-4B, so subtracting it from another system's block time leaves what that system's head costs. All six run together in each allocation, so the choice of machine cancels in the subtraction. We take the median block time over eight of the nine benchmarks, excluding HumanEval, whose short outputs let prefill dominate, and subtract one median from the other. Two things follow from measuring a difference rather than a stage. The figure is net of the per-slot argmax the control performs instead, which is the cost a deployment actually pays for reranking. And it resolves about 0.03 ms, the spread across three independent reads of the convolution's per-block cost, with per-benchmark head costs varying by up to $\pm 0.1$ ms around the median.

Precision. The drafter is trained with a full-precision master copy of its weights, and the optimizer moments are kept in full precision throughout. Two details follow from how that copy is handled. Some training runs stopped and resumed. On resume the drafter's weights are reloaded at the target model's precision, so the master copy is round-tripped through bf16 at that point, in resumed and uninterrupted runs alike. Where a resumed run re-covered steps it had already taken, the recomputed loss values matched the earlier pass to the precision logged. Separately, the drafter is initialized in full precision, but in the runs reported here that initialization was rounded to the target's precision before training began, so that arms differing only in precision started from numerically identical weights. The rounding moves the initialization only below bf16 resolution and leaves first-step loss and gradients unchanged.

DFlash2 is likewise served under both, and at its released selector width rather than at ours: matching the two candidate pools would change its method rather than control a variable, since the two rerankers are different mechanisms at different budgets, so what we match across arms is the drafted width instead. Each baseline is composed from its own released branch rather than reimplemented from its published settings, and DFlash2 specifically is benchmarked through a third-party reimplementation trained under our contract, since its own sources do not disclose a training recipe. All systems are trained on the same regenerated corpus for the same six epochs, at the same global batch size and sequence length, with self-distillation disabled on every arm, and with drafter and target sharing a rotary base of $10^{6}.$

## B Additional Results

Acceptance length and absolute throughput. Table 1 reports speedup, which is the quantity the comparison turns on. Tables 5 and 6 give the two underlying measurements for each target, the block-weighted acceptance length and the output throughput in tokens per second, under the same protocol. They are the source of the acceptance-length statements of Section 4.2.

Per-category results on SPEED. Tables 8 and 9 break the SPEED aggregate of Section 4.2 into its eleven categories, under the same protocol. The per-benchmark conclusions carry over: LiLiCorr serves faster than every system compared in all forty-four cells. The multilingual lead noted in Section 4.2 is the clearest of any category on both axes, reaching 7.4% in acceptance length and 6.3% in throughput on Qwen3-4B under greedy decoding. Sample standard deviations across the three $T=1$ seeds stay below 0.28 on acceptance length in every category and system, with one exception, roleplay on Qwen3-4B.

What scatter remains concentrates on the small splits, above all AIME 2025 and HumanEval, which at 30 and 164 prompts are the two smallest in the suite. ## C The Convolution Variant

DFlash2 contributes a grouped causal convolution inside the draft layers alongside its candidate selector. The two are independent: the convolution improves the drafter, and is indifferent to how the candidates it proposes are afterwards correlated.
